description: 🌎 Join Starcatchers! We’re a friendly team exploring Earth’s environmental changes using NASA data. We’d love to have curious, creative people join us! No experience needed, just bring your ideas and enthusiasm! 💚🚀
summary: EarthAlive is a map-based platform that turns NASA satellite and reanalysis data into clear trend answers. Users draw an area on a map, choose a variable such as land surface temperature or vegetation index, set a time range, and receive statistical trend tests, charts and a downloadable PDF report. Its comparison tools place variables side by side, such as vegetation against temperature, or one variable across several regions, so differences that a single chart would hide become visible. A rule-based guide helps new users set up their first analysis. The challenge asks for a tool that finds variables, visualises change and tests whether it is significant. EarthAlive does this, and its visual comparisons make patterns and anomalies easier to spot for scientists, students, decision-makers and citizens. The system is containerised with Docker, deployment-ready, and running as a live demo, so anyone can try it without installing anything. It matters because it turns open NASA data into evidence people can check and act on.
details:
What it does and how it works

EarthAlive is a full-stack platform that turns NASA satellite and reanalysis data into clear trend answers. A user draws an area of interest on a map, chooses one or more variables (land surface temperature, NDVI vegetation index, precipitation, soil moisture or air temperature), sets a time range, and selects statistical methods. The app returns trend direction, slope, statistical significance, charts, data-quality indicators and a downloadable PDF report.

Live deployment: https://earth-alive.vercel.app/

GitHub: https://github.com/ambientWave/NASA-MODIS-EarthAlive

How Does Our Solution Work

Earth Alive follows one path from question to evidence. A user asks a question, compares results across variables or places when needed, tracks the work in the background, and can get guidance from the built-in assistant at any point.

- Regular query: one location, one dataset

A single analysis answers one question about one area and one environmental variable. The user chooses a variable, a date range and a temporal resolution, then selects the statistical methods to run. The area of interest is drawn on the map, so the analysis is fully specified before it is submitted.

The result opens with headline indicators: the trend status, its significance, the data coverage and the number of valid observations. The analysis summary records the dataset, date range, area and methods. A data-quality panel shows missing observations and the observed range, so readers can judge whether the result is reliable before they read the charts.

Each method has its own diagnostic chart with a plain-language explanation. A regression plot shows the observed values with the fitted trend line and reports the slope, p-value, R² and sample size. A Mann-Kendall plot reports the test statistic, Kendall's tau and p-value. Where a trend is not statistically significant, the tool reports it as uncertain rather than as a confirmed change.

Every finished analysis can be exported as a PDF report. It summarises the job details, key indicators and trend chart, along with the spatial view of the area, so the result can be shared without the app. The report lets students, planners and colleagues keep and share a result without needing the app.

- Comparison: one location with several datasets, or several locations with one dataset

Comparison answers questions that a single chart cannot. In variable comparison, the user selects two to five variables for the same area and period, and the results show how they move together. This helps the user see whether a change in one variable is linked to a change in another.

In region comparison, the user picks a benchmark variable and selects up to eight regions on the map, either by drawing them or from preset regions. Each region is analysed against the same variable and period, so differences between places are visible at once.

- Jobs: tracking the work

Analyses run in the background, so the app stays responsive while data is processed. The Jobs page lists each run with its type, a short ID, its status and its creation time. Finished jobs can be opened to view results or exported as PDF reports. The list can be filtered by status: active, finished, canceled or failed.

- Assistant: guided help for new users

The Analysis Assistant leads a user through the same steps as a regular query, without requiring prior knowledge of the options. It offers preset scenarios and a custom analysis path, and each answer leads to the next step, from choosing an area and time range to submitting the job. It is a rule-based workflow built on canned questions.

Who it is for

- Students and educators, who can learn from real Earth data.

- Scientists and researchers, who can screen many regions and variables quickly and spot trends, patterns and anomalies before deeper analysis.

- Decision-makers, such as city planners, agricultural advisers, water and disaster managers and policy officials, who need evidence of where conditions are changing.

- Journalists and citizens, who want to check environmental claims.

The challenge came from difficulties that scientists face, so the tool is meant to make expert work easier, not only to teach. Built-in guidance, an FAQ and a glossary keep it accessible to newcomers.

Benefits

- Faster exploration: from a drawn area to a tested trend without writing code or handling raw rasters.

- Consistent, repeatable results, because the same tests run every time.

- Transparent quality: every result reports sample count, missing data and warnings, and the system declines to give a verdict when data is too sparse, too short or nearly constant.

- Easy sharing: a PDF report for every finished analysis.

- Easy start: a rule-based guided workflow with canned questions and example scenarios (for example an Egypt vegetation trend) helps first-time users. It is not AI.

Intended impact

We hope EarthAlive helps scientists find trends, patterns and anomalies faster, helps decision-makers see where heat, vegetation or rainfall is changing, and helps students and citizens learn from open NASA data. It is meant as a tool for explorers who want to understand, and change, the world. It is open source and containerised with Docker, so other teams and institutions can run their own instances.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

- Frontend: Flutter and Dart, flutter_bloc, flutter_map, fl_chart, dio.

- Backend: Python, FastAPI, Uvicorn, Pydantic v2, Redis, RQ.

- Data and analysis: NASA AppEEARS API, NumPy, pandas, SciPy, Matplotlib.

- Testing: pytest (unit, endpoint and integration tests).

- Deployment: Docker and Docker Compose, with separate containers for API, workers and Redis. The system is deployment-ready and running as a live demo.

- Hardware: VPS.

Creativity

The challenge asks for a tool that finds a variable, pulls its data, plots a time series and tests the trend's significance. EarthAlive meets that brief and goes further:

- Side-by-side comparison of variables and regions, so patterns and anomalies are easier to spot than in single charts.

- A PDF report for every analysis, so results travel beyond the app.

- A guided workflow that walks new users through choosing a variable, drawing an area, setting dates and methods, and submitting, with example scenarios to try first.

Factors the team considered

- Scientific validity: non-parametric tests for non-normal data, corrections for autocorrelation and seasonality, and minimum-data checks.

- Accessibility: one codebase for phones, tablets and desktops, with plain-language guidance.

- Reproducibility: containerised deployment, a documented API and tests across the pipeline.

- Honesty about limits: our demonstrations use short sample periods, so they show that the tool works rather than proving long-term climate change. Significance shows a change, not its cause.

- Data access: we began with direct granule access through earthaccess, then moved to the AppEEARS API to avoid a system-level GDAL dependency. This simplified deployment but required harmonising products, so every result reports the product, version and granularity it used.
